extracted.intended_audience: chemists and chemistry students (experimental chemists, late-18th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and principles for designing and interpreting combustion and decomposition experiments (measurement of heat, stoichiometry, apparatus, repeatability) plus a proposed systematic nomenclature for oxides and acids in vegetal and animal substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ice-calorimeter measurement of caloric (quantify heat by ice melted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the caloric evolved in combustion by using an apparatus surrounded by ice and express the heat as the quantity (weight) of ice melted (e.g., 'quantité de livres de glace qu'il peut fondre').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give caloric results in units of melted ice (pounds/onces/gros/grains where used), report per unit mass of combustible and per unit mass of oxygen when appropriate; note practical limits (e.g., caloric contained in hydrogen gas may be impossible to account for in some experiments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report reactant/product quantities and caloric per component
rubrics_metrics.description: For each combustion, present the measured masses of reactants (combustible and oxygen) and products, and compute caloric released per pound of combustible and per pound of oxygen (as done for phosphorus, charcoal, hydrogen gas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide tabular breakdowns showing quantities before/after reaction and derived caloric numbers so others can reproduce calculations; include units and intermediate arithmetic as in the examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and justify experimental assumptions about retained caloric
rubrics_metrics.description: When computing caloric balances, explicitly state assumptions such as 'one supposes here that the phosphoric acid retains no portion of caloric', while acknowledging this may not be rigorously true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate when an assumption is made for lack of direct measurement, estimate the likely magnitude of error if possible, and mark results conditional on these assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale apparatus and method to magnitude of heat release
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose experimental scale and apparatus according to expected heat evolved; combinations that release very little heat (e.g., combination of nitrous gas and oxygen to form nitric/nitrous acid) require very large/complex apparatus or alternative calculation-based approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If direct calorimetric measurement would produce an undetectably small temperature change, either operate on a much larger scale with cumbersome equipment (e.g., apparatus in ice) or supplement with theoretical/calculated estimates validated by other experiments (e.g., detonations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use detonation/indirect experiments when direct measurement is impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: Where direct combination experiments are impractical due to small heat release, perform related experiments (such as controlled detonations) and use composition analysis plus proportional reasoning to infer caloric contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: infer the caloric contribution of oxygen in nitric acid formation from detonation of saltpetre with charcoal, combined with compositional analysis of saltpetre to scale results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic nomenclature for oxides and acids (vegetal/animal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose naming oxides and acids according to the nature of their acidifiable bases (e.g., oxide hydro-carboneux, acide hydro-carbonique oxygéné), reflecting which principles (hydrogen, carbon, phosphorus, nitrogen, oxygen) compose the base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer multiple variant forms to indicate subtle differences (e.g., oxide hydro-carboneux vs oxide hydro-carbonique) and use term structure to show which principle is in excess; retain clarity that nomenclature should reflect composition when known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffix convention to indicate oxygen vs base predominance (-eux vs -ique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate names of acids by endings: terminate with -eux for those suspected to have the acidifiable base in excess, and -ique when oxygen is predominant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this convention pragmatically to animal acids/oxides where composition suggests one or the other, but avoid forcing systematic names before compositions are reliably determined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic retention of traditional names until compositions are precise
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep ancient/traditional names for complex acids and oxides until experiments yield sufficiently precise compositional data to justify systematic renaming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when proposing a systematic nomenclature, be conservative: only adopt new names when the science precedes the language and compositions are well established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and naming of combinations among combustibles
rubrics_metrics.description: When combustible substances combine without prior oxygenation, name them as sulfures (sulfides), phosphures (phosphides), carbures (carbides), and for hydrogenated gaseous combinations use gas hydrogène carboné/sulfuré/phosphoré.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend the naming pattern to alkaline combinations (e.g., 'sulfure de potasse') and use consistent terminology across examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alloy/amalgam characterization and expected physical behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe alloys as combinations of metals with possible degrees of saturation; differences in metals' fusibility typically cause particular properties (e.g., brittleness when a lower-melting component liquefies on heating). Mercury–metal combinations are designated 'amalgames'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When characterizing alloys, consider degree of saturation, relative fusibility of constituents, and predict mechanical properties (malleability when cold, brittleness when heated) from those differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fixed versus volatile oils by heating behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed oils (from plants) contain excess carbon that separates on heating beyond boiling water temperatures; volatile (essential) oils have proportions that prevent decomposition at such temperatures and instead form gaseous products when combined with caloric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use heating/distillation tests to classify oils: fixed oils decompose on strong heating producing free carbon; volatile oils pass into gas (with caloric) and are recovered by distillation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine oil composition via combustion results and mass balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer oil composition (proportions of hydrogen and carbon) by burning known mass in oxygen and applying calorimetric and stoichiometric analysis (example given: some oils composed of ~21 parts hydrogen and 79 parts carbon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine calorimetric data (ice melted), measured masses of reactants/products, and known behaviors on distillation to estimate elemental composition; treat early figures as provisional pending replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperature-dependent decomposition governed by affinities
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret thermal decomposition of vegetal/animal matter by relative affinities of hydrogen, oxygen, and carbon and the amount of caloric: below water-boiling-level heat favors H+O→water and oil formation; red heat favors O+carbon→acid carbonique (CO2) and liberation of hydrogen as gas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments and interpret products with attention to applied heat level ('chaleur rouge' vs near boiling); expect qualitatively different decomposition pathways at different temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude moisture rigorously to avoid misattributing hydrogen evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: In experiments testing if hydrogen combines with metals in the solid state, traces of moisture can produce hydrogen by water decomposition; more careful drying tends to reduce observed hydrogen, indicating contamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply very strict drying and moisture exclusion techniques in metal–hydrogen combination experiments to avoid false positives; interpret any residual hydrogen cautiously and consider alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat experiments and report provisional status of early results
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that initial determinations are often approximate; repeat and multiply experiments to obtain exact quantities and be prepared to correct earlier results when more precise data are obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat preliminary 'à-peu-près' results as useful starting points for others; explicitly state where further replication is needed and where numerical uncertainties may be significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control vessel size and heating rate in distillation/rectification
rubrics_metrics.description: Vessel capacity and the degree/rapidity of heating affect rectification and decomposition outcomes: small vessels and gentle heat slow decomposition; large vessels and stronger heat accelerate breakdown of oils to water and carbon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning distillations and rectifications, choose vessel size and heating regimen to either preserve volatile components or to drive decomposition, and report those parameters when presenting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerate known acids/oxides as current state of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: List the currently known vegetable acids (thirteen enumerated) and animal acids (six enumerated) and classify them by their principal bases (hydrogen, carbon, phosphorus, nitrogen, oxygen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such enumerations to situate new experimental findings relative to contemporary knowledge, but note that lists are provisional and subject to revision as compositions become better known.
